planting.note: Root large truncheon (branch-tip) cuttings in spring in a lean, extremely fast-draining mix before planting out, or start from container-grown seedlings; this is the largest species in the genus and needs decades of frost-free growth to become the branching, elephant-legged tree it is prized for.

directions: Tree aloe is the tallest species in the genus, developing a thick, gray, elephant-hide trunk that can eventually reach 30-60 feet in habitat and forks into a broad, sparsely branched crown far taller than the multi-stemmed torch aloe or the single-trunked Cape aloe grown elsewhere in this collection. Native to subtropical thicket and forest margins from KwaZulu-Natal through Mozambique, it carries narrow gray-green rosettes only at the branch tips, with dusty rose-pink flower spikes appearing in winter once the tree is mature. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and plenty of overhead and lateral room to grow, since it is usually planted as a single specimen tree rather than massed with other succulents. Growth is extremely slow for the first ten to twenty years, but established plants are long-lived, drought tolerant, and become genuine landscape trees in zone 9b-11 gardens.

planting.note: Plant nursery starts in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; snake aloe grows solitary and does not offset, so it is propagated from seed rather than from pups.

directions: Snake aloe forms a single stemless rosette of broad, blue-green leaves edged in reddish-brown teeth that curve inward near the tip, a highveld grassland species from the Free State, Eastern Cape, and Lesotho that tolerates frost and even occasional snow better than most aloes in cultivation. Its most distinctive feature is the flower spike itself: densely overlapping bracts hide the small cream to pale yellow-brown flowers until they emerge, giving the spike a tightly scaled, almost reptilian texture that is the source of the common name. Unlike clumping species such as soap aloe or Cape aloe, it never offsets and must be grown from seed, staying a single rosette for its entire life. Site it on a slope or raised bed with excellent drainage, since its highland origin makes it more cold-tolerant but no more tolerant of wet feet than any other aloe.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; tilt-head aloe develops a single upright trunk over several years and, unlike torch aloe or tree aloe, does not branch or sucker.

directions: Tilt-head aloe takes its common name from the way its winter flower spike bends distinctly to one side as it lengthens, unlike the upright candelabra spikes of Cape aloe or torch aloe grown elsewhere in this collection. A single, unbranched trunk carries ascending gray-green leaves lined with fine reddish-brown marginal teeth, eventually reaching 10-15 feet in an Eastern Cape thicket habitat. Flowers open cream to pale pink with conspicuous protruding stamens and produce copious nectar, making it one of the most valuable winter forage plants for sunbirds in its native range and for hummingbirds where it is grown in California and the Gulf Coast. Give it full sun and sharp drainage and expect a slow but steady rise to a striking single-stemmed specimen over four to eight years.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; French aloe is one of the few aloes that thrives under high, open tree canopy rather than demanding full desert sun.

directions: French aloe is a multi-stemmed, branching species from forest margins and coastal scrub in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, and unlike almost every other tree-form aloe in this collection it tolerates and even prefers light shade beneath a high canopy, a trait tied to its forest-edge origin. Its glossy, bright green leaves carry fine, soft white marginal teeth that are noticeably less fierce than the heavy spines of Cape aloe or torch aloe, and the common name fence aloe comes from its historical use as a living, impenetrable hedge along Eastern Cape farm boundaries. Salmon to coral-red tubular flowers appear on branched spikes in late winter, drawing sunbirds and bees. It branches and suckers from the base over time, gradually forming a large, multi-trunked clump 8-15 feet tall that works well as a shade-garden accent in frost-free climates.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun; dune aloe is naturally salt- and wind-tolerant, making it a good choice for exposed coastal sites where other large aloes struggle.

directions: Dune aloe grows wild on the coastal dunes of KwaZulu-Natal, where constant salt spray and wind have shaped a naturally salt-tolerant plant well suited to seaside gardens where most other large aloes struggle. A single stem, often leaning with age, carries broad, wavy, recurved gray-green leaves and eventually reaches 6-12 feet. It is also one of the later-flowering large aloes, producing bright orange spikes in autumn rather than the midwinter bloom typical of Cape aloe, torch aloe, and tilt-head aloe, extending the aloe flowering season into a period when few other species are in bloom. Plant in full sun with sandy, sharply drained soil, and expect it to be markedly more cold-sensitive than highveld or Karoo species since it comes from a frost-free subtropical coastline.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring on a rocky, sharply drained slope in full sun; peglerae aloe is a slow-growing, mostly solitary species best treated as a specimen collector's plant rather than a mass-planting groundcover.

directions: Peglerae aloe forms a tight, nearly spherical rosette of broad leaves that curve strongly inward toward the center, a growth habit distinct enough from every other aloe here that it looks almost like a leafy artichoke rather than a typical open rosette. It is native to rocky quartzite ridges of the Magaliesberg mountains in South Africa's Gauteng and North West provinces, where cold nights and rocky, ultra-fast drainage are the norm, giving it more cold tolerance than most lowland aloes. Dense, felted reddish-brown to salmon flower heads appear in winter atop short stalks, distinct from the tall open spikes of species like tilt-head or snake aloe. It is classified as endangered in the wild due to illegal collection, offsets slowly if at all, and rewards patient growers with a genuinely unusual architectural form on a rock garden or trough.
sources: Red List of South African Plants (SANBI)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; zebra aloe is one of the more summer-rainfall-tolerant aloes and can handle occasional wet-season humidity better than strictly winter-rainfall Cape species.

directions: Zebra aloe carries bold, elongated H-shaped white markings across the undersides of its gray-green leaves, a bolder and more geometric pattern than the fine white speckling of little spotted aloe or the raised ridges of coral aloe grown elsewhere in this collection. Widespread across the savannas of Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Botswana, and South Africa's Limpopo and Mpumalanga provinces, it is well adapted to summer-rainfall climates and tolerates more warm-season humidity than many winter-rainfall Cape aloes. Clumping rather than solitary, it offsets steadily at the base to form a low colony, sending up orange-red tubular flower spikes above the foliage in winter. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage; it is frost-tender and best suited to zone 9-11 gardens or container culture farther north.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant nursery starts in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; little spotted aloe flushes reddish-purple in cold or dry stress, so hold back water in winter to intensify its color.

directions: Little spotted aloe carries fine, densely scattered white spots across both leaf surfaces, a smaller and more uniform speckling than the larger, more irregular blotches of soap aloe, and its leaf color shifts dramatically from green to burgundy or purplish-brown under winter cold, drought stress, or intense sun. Native to the Little Karoo and surrounding Eastern and Western Cape regions of South Africa, it is usually solitary or forms only small, loose clusters rather than spreading into the broad colonies typical of soap aloe. Its winter to early-spring flower spikes are notably bicolor, opening from red-orange buds at the base of the raceme to clear yellow flowers near the tip, so a single spike shows both colors at once. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage and let the soil dry between waterings to encourage the deepest winter color.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online
